concepts.name: Spotting the pattern from the problem statement
Why mix patterns in one practice session
Structure of a timed attempt before you code

questions.prompt: "Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters." Which pattern does this point to?

choices.text: Sort the characters, then use two pointers from both ends
A min-heap of size k
A sliding window with a set of the characters in the window
Binary search on the string

questions.explanation: A question about the longest contiguous substring or subarray under a condition is the classic sliding-window signal: two pointers moving in the same direction. Sorting would destroy the order that defines a substring. A heap is the signal for "top k" questions.

sources.title: Built-in Types
sources.claim: A set is an unordered collection of distinct hashable objects used for membership testing and removing duplicates, and str is an immutable sequence whose contiguous substrings are slices s[i:j].

questions.prompt: "Return the k most frequent elements." Which approach does the problem statement suggest?

choices.text: A sliding window over the array, tracking counts as it moves
Count with a hash map, then keep a heap of size k
Two pointers after sorting the array by value
Breadth-first search over a graph of the values

questions.explanation: The Tech Interview Handbook says a "top or lowest k" in the question usually signals a heap. First count frequencies in a hash map, then keep the k best in a heap. Sliding windows are for contiguous ranges, which this problem doesn't have.

sources.title: collections — Container datatypes
sources.claim: Counter is a dict subclass for counting hashable objects, and most_common(n) returns the n elements with the highest counts.

sources.title: heapq — Heap queue algorithm
sources.claim: heapq implements a min-heap with the smallest item at heap[0], and heapq.nlargest(n, iterable, key) returns the n largest items and performs best for small n.

sources.title: Heap cheatsheet for coding interviews | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: A top or lowest k in the question usually signals a heap, with Top K Frequent Elements cited as the example.

questions.prompt: "Merge all overlapping intervals." What first step makes one pass over the intervals enough?

choices.text: Sort the intervals by their start value
Put every interval into a hash set
Sort the intervals by their length
Build a heap keyed on end values and pop until empty

questions.explanation: After sorting by start, any interval that overlaps the last merged one comes right after it. So one pass can either extend the last merged interval or start a new one. The handbook calls sorting by start crucial to Merge Intervals. Sorting by length doesn't put overlapping intervals next to each other.

sources.title: Sorting Techniques
sources.claim: sorted() and list.sort() accept a key function, such as one returning an interval's start value, and sorts are guaranteed stable.

sources.title: Interval cheatsheet for coding interviews | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: Sorting intervals by start value is a common routine for interval questions and is crucial to solving Merge Intervals.

questions.prompt: You find the k largest of n numbers by pushing each onto a min-heap and popping whenever the heap grows past k. What is the time complexity?

choices.text: O(n log n)
O(k log n)
O(n · k)
O(n log k)

questions.explanation: The heap never holds more than k items, so each push or pop costs O(log k), done for n elements: O(n log k). Sorting everything would be O(n log n), which is worse when k is much smaller than n.

sources.title: heapq — Heap queue algorithm
sources.claim: Python's heapq is a min-heap whose smallest element is always at heap[0], so popping removes the smallest of the kept items.

questions.prompt:
What is the time complexity of this function for a string of length n?

```python
def longest_unique(s):
    seen = set()
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        while ch in seen:
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(ch)
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

choices.text: O(n²), because the inner `while` loop is nested inside the `for` loop
O(n), because `left` only moves forward, at most n times in total
O(n log n), because each set insert and removal costs O(log n)
O(2ⁿ), because it effectively checks every possible substring

questions.explanation: The `while` loop looks nested, but across the whole run `left` only increases and never passes `right`, so it moves at most n times in total. Each character is added once and removed at most once, with average O(1) set operations: O(n) overall. `longest_unique("abcabcbb")` returns 3.

sources.title: TimeComplexity - Python Wiki
sources.claim: Membership testing 'x in s' on a Python set is O(1) in the average case.

questions.prompt: Compare the brute-force solution to "longest substring without repeating characters" with the sliding-window solution. Explain where the time saving comes from.

model_answer.summary: Brute force checks every substring, so it needs at least O(n²) time. The sliding window keeps a window with no repeats, where each character enters and leaves at most once, giving O(n) with average O(1) set lookups.
key_points: Brute force looks at all O(n²) substrings, and checking each for repeats costs more on top
The sliding window's two pointers only move forward and never cross
Each index enters the window once and leaves it at most once, so the total work is O(n)
A hash set gives average O(1) membership checks, and its extra space is bounded by the window size or the alphabet

questions.explanation: The handbook describes the sliding window as two pointers moving in the same direction that never overtake each other, which keeps it O(n). Saying the nested loop is O(n²) is the common mistake: count the total moves of the pointers, not the loops.

questions.prompt: Why solve three medium problems from different patterns in one session, instead of three sliding-window problems in a row?

choices.text: You must identify each problem's type and pick a method, which blocked practice lets you skip
Mixed practice gets you through more problems per hour, since each one feels fresh
Dunlosky's review rated interleaving the single most effective learning technique
Interviews always ask the patterns in a fixed order, and mixed practice rehearses that exact order

questions.explanation: Interleaved practice mixes different kinds of problems in one session. Dunlosky explains that it makes learners tell problem types apart and pick the right strategy, while blocked practice lets them apply one method almost without thinking. His review rated interleaving moderate utility; practice testing and distributed practice were rated high.

sources.title: Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning
sources.publisher: American Federation of Teachers, American Educator (John Dunlosky)
sources.claim: Interleaving forces learners to work out which kind of problem each is and what steps to take, while massed practice lets them apply the same steps robotically; interleaving was rated moderate (promising) while practice testing and distributed practice were rated high.

sources.title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
sources.publisher: Association for Psychological Science (Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan, Willingham)
sources.claim: The review rated practice testing and distributed practice as the high-utility techniques.

questions.prompt: Your problem log shows five sliding-window problems solved easily in a row, then a failure on a mixed set. Explain what happened and how you would change your practice.

model_answer.summary: In a block of similar problems you already knew the method, so you practised applying it but not choosing it. Mixed sets train you to recognise the problem type, which is what an interview requires.
key_points: Blocked practice lets you apply the same method without identifying the problem type
Interleaved practice mixes problem kinds, so you must first work out which method fits
An interview problem doesn't come labelled with its pattern
Keep sessions mixed, and log the cue in each problem that should have signalled its pattern

questions.explanation: This is the effect interleaving research describes: blocked practice feels easier and hides the missing skill of choosing a strategy. Logging the signal ("contiguous range", "top k") turns each miss into a cue for next time.

sources.title: Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning
sources.publisher: American Federation of Teachers, American Educator (John Dunlosky)
sources.claim: Massed (blocked) practice gives better performance during practice but lets learners skip identifying the problem type; interleaved practice outperforms it on delayed tests.

questions.prompt: The timer starts on a medium problem. According to the Tech Interview Handbook's checklist, what should you do before writing any code?

choices.text: Write the brute-force code straight away, so there's working code on screen early
Write pseudocode for the whole solution, then translate it line by line into code
Write the edge-case tests first, so the code you write afterwards is test-driven from the start
Clarify the question, work a small example, then outline approaches with their complexity

questions.explanation: The checklist says to paraphrase the question, clarify assumptions and input ranges, and work through a simplified example. Then explain a few approaches at a high level with their time and space complexity, and only start coding once the approach is agreed. It also asks for real, working code rather than pseudocode.

sources.title: Coding interview cheatsheet: Best practices before, during and after | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: Before coding, paraphrase the question, clarify assumptions and input ranges, work a simplified example, explain approaches with their time and space complexity, and get agreement; then write working code, not pseudocode.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would spend the first few minutes of a timed 30-minute attempt, before you type any code, and why each step saves time later.

model_answer.summary: Restate and clarify the problem, check it on a small example, then outline candidate approaches with their complexity. Code only once you have chosen one. Each step catches a misunderstanding or a dead end while it is still cheap to fix.
key_points: Paraphrase the problem and clarify assumptions and the input range
Work a small example by hand to confirm you understood it
Outline one or more approaches, with time and space complexity, and pick one
Start coding only after the approach is chosen, so you don't rewrite halfway through

questions.explanation: These steps are the handbook's before-coding and during-coding checklist. Its prep guide also budgets about 30 minutes per question. Skipping them is the usual reason a timed attempt fails: a misread problem or a wrong approach found only after the code is written.

sources.title: Coding interview cheatsheet: Best practices before, during and after | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The checklist has you clarify the question, work a simplified example, and explain approaches with time and space complexity before starting to code.

sources.title: Coding interviews: Everything you need to prepare | Tech Interview Handbook
sources.claim: The prep guide plans practice at about 30 minutes per question, and says interview rounds typically last 30-45 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which facts explain a set-based sliding-window algorithm for unique substrings? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Both window pointers move forward rather than restarting for each substring.
Each duplicate requires rescanning every previous substring from scratch.
Each character enters once and leaves at most once.
Average constant-time set operations allow linear total scanning work.
Enumerating all possible substrings yields only a linear number of candidates.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: monotonic pointers avoid repeating the whole scan. B: Incorrect: advancing the left boundary removes duplicates incrementally. C: Correct: there are at most two boundary operations per character. D: Correct: the linear number of operations gives expected O(n) time. E: Incorrect: an n-character string has n(n+1)/2 contiguous substring candidates.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe interleaved problem-solving practice? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It mixes problem types so learners must identify the needed method.
Blocked practice can feel fluent while hiding weak pattern recognition.
Solving one repeated type proves transfer to unfamiliar mixed problems.
Interleaving guarantees better immediate practice scores in every session.
Delayed-test performance can improve despite harder practice sessions.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: choosing the procedure becomes part of the practice. B: Correct: repeatedly applying one method can avoid identifying the problem. C: Incorrect: repeated same-type performance does not demonstrate method selection. D: Incorrect: the cited study found higher immediate performance under blocked practice. E: Correct: interleaving improved later test performance in the reported research.

questions.prompt: Which steps belong before coding a timed interview solution? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Start typing immediately and postpone all input assumptions until testing.
Clarify ambiguous requirements and the input constraints.
Work through a small example to check your understanding.
Explain candidate approaches and their time and space costs.
Choose an approach only after implementing every possible alternative.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: clarifying assumptions first avoids coding the wrong problem. B: Correct: the interview checklist explicitly recommends clarification. C: Correct: a simplified example helps validate the intended behavior. D: Correct: discussing costs supports selecting a suitable approach. E: Incorrect: choose and communicate an approach before implementation.
